text:
Harry Kane speaking to UEFA about his time at FC Bayern so far:

"When I arrived, I didn't know what to expect. I'd been at Tottenham for so long. Obviously, I knew, coming in, there would be expectations for me to score and be the No9, but it's been even beyond what I thought. I've loved every minute of it; I've loved the expectation, the pressure of being here, the expectation to win every season. But [there are] still more moments that I want to achieve and more goals that I want to achieve, and [winning] the Champions League is definitely one of those.

The reception I've had here in Germany has been incredible – not just for me, but, I think, for my family as well. And, you know, even for this World Cup, for example, when Germany went out of the World Cup, I had so many people from Germany who said: "We're now supporting England. We want you to do well and you to win." Before I'd ever come, I never thought that would be possible. I think they appreciate me as a person and me as a player."

text:
这是我近期看到最有价值的文章，分享给大家
来自沃顿商学院对 AI 时代如何进行开发的讨论

> 他们打造了一个 AI 工作室（Generative AI Studio），来观察学生们如何通过 AI 去制作项目。

他们观察到，有两种典型的协作模式会限制学生的创造力。
1. 学生们总是随时准备行动，迫不及待地把想法变成现实，但是这会过早地将他们的精力集中在执行上，而非发明创造上。
2. 当学生们在一起讨论的时候，群体思维迅速出现，它会让平庸的想法被不断附和、放大，而真正原创的想法反而变少了

同时，学生们对待 AI 的态度也非常典型：
1. 学生把 AI 当成自动售货机，以为丢一句简单提示词就能得到完美成品，不会去管理 AI 随机性，没有耐心通过持续沟通、补充上下文、逐步纠偏来得到好结果。
2. 把 AI 当成只会写代码的工具。有一位学生想做一款健身 APP，他一开始就沉浸到如何设计数据库、保存训练数据上面，没有思考如何用 AI 去创造那些普通 APP 做不到的体验。

对此，沃顿商学院的教师们提出了解决方案

判断力、品味、创造力和批判性思维仍然是 AI 时代最宝贵的特质，他们从这一点出发，设计了 Crit（作品评议）以及 Charrette（一日限时创作）

Crit——培养判断力

你可以把它理解成作品互评论，有两种形式：

1. 1 对 1 crit：导师直接给反馈，指出哪里需要加强、哪里是亮点、需不需要换方向、要不要返工等细节。
2. 小组 crit：在导师的主持下，让同伴之间进行互评

不管哪种形式，开场都一样：学生先展示作品，然后向全场征集反馈。展示时要说清五件事——

1. 我的意图（想做什么）
2. 我的制作过程
3. 过程中有什么新发现
4. 冒出了什么新问题
5. 还剩下什么挑战

为了控制评论的质量，避免把互评变成宣判大会，导师要求所有的评价意见以这三种句式开头：
1. "I notice…"（我注意到……）——先慢慢看、仔细看，描述你想讨论的东西，而不是直接下结论
2. "I wonder…?"（我在想……？）——用问题开启对话，而不是用判决关闭对话
3. "What if…?"（如果……会怎样？）——把替代方向当作"可能性"提出来，帮对方推进他自己的目标或抓住意外机会

一个实际的例子是：
一个学生想做健身 App，他的思路很常规：问卷调查 + 询问健身房器材 + AI 出训练计划。在 Crit 中有人追问："AI 能不能做出普通 App 做不到的体验？"这个问题直接推翻了预设：不需要器材数据库，用户拍一张眼前环境的照片，AI 就能理解现场条件、生成真正个性化的训练方案。
这个例子非常有说服力，因为我经常去酒店的健身房，如果有这样的 APP，我真的会使用的。

拓展起来，我们到团队或者公司里面，其实也可以用这种方式去互评，非常有参考价值。

Charrette —— 培养创作流程

Charrette 的过程一共有 6 步

1. 开场设定问题
2. 个人独立用纸笔发散大量粗糙想法
3. 全班梳理筛选，对上一步的想法进行评审，最后决定开发哪些产品
4. 2–3 人小队只做规划，不涉及任何执行
5. 使用 AI，限时两个小时做出原型
6. 全班展示评议

整个过程限定在 8 个小时，其中制作部分最多只有两个小时。

这是整篇文章我最喜欢的部分，如果你做过开发，你很容易发现自己花了大量的时间在执行工作上，甚至好几天好几夜都停不下来。但是别人问起你有没有产品原型可以体验的时候，你经常发现自己拿不出来。

Charrette 的目的是，让学生们意识到，AI 时代规划的工作是比执行工作更重要的，因为 AI 能够帮你去执行，你不应该再把自己放在执行者的位置上。但是 AI 却不能取代你的创造力和批判性思维，所以你更应该给自己一些时间，去思考问题，思考解决方案，而不是急着去动手。

非常棒的文章，值得分享给大家，原文链接：

https://t.co/46EI9gp7hY

team landed a bunch of updates to dots  🙌

new things:
- create your dot on iOS / Android + open ChatGPT straight into it
- kick off Codex work and follow up on threads, with context from your chats, Codex threads and automations

- Enterprise web + voice access fixes

keep the feedback coming!!

text:
just hit $545k MRR... still the only full-time dev 

and the app is over 1m lines of code...

in the last 7 days i merged 1,089 PRs 

here's the tech stack..

1. over 50 oh-my-pi agents running in parallel on my home linux server

2. 8 Max Claude plans, 1 SuperGrok Heavy plan, and 5 max Codex plans

3. Slack & Telegram to communicate with my bots. I no longer use a terminal or IDE

4. Linear, the central PM tool my bots use for issue tracking. Every engineering request, bug report, alert and error gets posted here

5. Supabase staging database + Railway preview environments for testing

6. Ubicloud runners for GitHub Actions

7. 4 Mac minis as self-hosted runners for iOS builds and 15 end-to-end iPhone journey tests

8. Sentry for error monitoring

9. pstack by @poteto, my main agent uses her orchestrate playbook to manage the other 50 sessions. it never touches code.

10. a custom 5-stage planning harness before any code gets written.

11. customized pr-af and codex for independent code reviews, so that the model that wrote the code never passes it

12. greptile for final code reviews

13. a watcher that tracks every web merge in production for 24 hours, and reverts it on its own if real users start failing

Grok Bot 这种云端 Bot 功能还是太弱鸡。比我自己本地的 Mac Studio 上完善的基础设施差远了。

我家里的 Mac Studio M4 Max 上运行了：Tailscale + Tmux + oMLX + MFLUX + Paseo  + Paseo Bots + Chrome( CDP 端口打开) + Syncthing + Parsec + Obsidian。

我可以通过手机，iPad，MacBook 从任意地点随时随地访问这些基础设置，而且还是 7*24 运行的。

Grok Bot 可以每天访问 1000 次 X 原生 API 接口。但我也能本地通过 Paseo + Grok Build 去调，然后在 Paseo Bots里面去自动化使用。

所以看起来，Grok Bot 目前对我没啥吸引力，又或者是我本地这套基础设施搭得太顺手了。

text:
我近些年反复强调，AI Agent设计芯片比软件简单1万倍。

VLSI design内部有大量test规则，大量formal verification，大量simulation和verification的规则，所有芯片都必须走一遍，这个场景是天生适合AI Agent重复去做，不用human in the loop。

软件开发才是更麻烦的， 今天张姐跑过来，喊你给HR系统加个功能，明天孙姐让你把某个layout挪一挪，后天王大胖子要你把某个部件的所有功能放在database里方便tracking和restore，每天高强度human in the loop。

就这个道理，绝大多数程序员是想不明白的，这个年代傻逼才学EE，傻逼才读razavi的书刷VLSI的课程，因为这个行业被党哥的RSI Chip一锅端的概率，比程序员被AI Agent替代的概率大得多。

党哥就是大反派，RSI Chip就是让AI Agent完成一切VLSI design、testbench、simulation、verification的工作，让芯片设计产业彻底由AI Agent和极少数顶级EECS复合型人才（和平区户籍）接管。

以后饭碗一定会彻底砸个精光，清华电子电气电机的，Stanford和UC Berkeley VLSI的，都他妈给我下车间调试PLC去。

text:
If I had to pass an AI engineer technical interview in the next 24 hours, I'd practice these 25 problems.

They cover 95% of the concepts.

1) Design a RAG system for 10M documents
2) Your RAG gives wrong answers. Debug it
3) Pick a chunking strategy for legal contracts
4) BM25 vs dense vs hybrid search: when to use each
5) Add a reranker and measure if it helped
6) Reduce LLM cost by 70% without hurting quality
7) Cut first-token latency for a chat app
8) Design a semantic cache with hit-rate tracking
9) Route requests between a cheap and a smart model
10) Build an agent that uses tools reliably
11) Your agent gets stuck in a loop. Fix it
12) Design memory for a long-running assistant
13) Make LLM output always valid JSON
14) Detect and reduce hallucinations
15) Build an eval suite for a customer support bot
16) LLM-as-a-judge: how to make it trustworthy
17) Block prompt injection in a tool-using agent
18) Redact PII before it hits the model
19) Fine-tune vs RAG vs prompting: pick one and defend it
20) Fine-tune a small model with LoRA on 5K examples
21) Serve an open model at scale (batching, KV cache, quantization)
22) Stream responses over SSE and handle disconnects
23) Trace every step of a multi-agent workflow
24) Roll back a bad prompt change in production
25) Design ChatGPT-style chat for 1M daily users

Don't memorize answers.
Practice explaining trade-offs out loud.

That's what interviewers actually grade.

Bookmark this. You'll need it before your next interview.

1) Design a RAG system for 10M documents
2) Your RAG gives wrong answers. Debug it
3) Pick a chunking strategy for legal contracts
4) BM25 vs dense vs hybrid search: when to use each
5) Add a reranker and measure if it helped
6) Reduce LLM cost by 70% without hurting quality
7) Cut first-token latency for a chat app
8) Design a semantic cache with hit-rate tracking
9) Route requests between a cheap and a smart model
10) Build an agent that uses tools reliably
11) Your agent gets stuck in a loop. Fix it
12) Design memory for a long-running assistant
13) Make LLM output always valid JSON
14) Detect and reduce hallucinations
15) Build an eval suite for a customer support bot
16) LLM-as-a-judge: how to make it trustworthy
17) Block prompt injection in a tool-using agent
18) Redact PII before it hits the model
19) Fine-tune vs RAG vs prompting: pick one and defend it
20) Fine-tune a small model with LoRA on 5K examples
21) Serve an open model at scale (batching, KV cache, quantization)
22) Stream responses over SSE and handle disconnects
23) Trace every step of a multi-agent workflow
24) Roll back a bad prompt change in production
25) Design ChatGPT-style chat for 1M daily users

Don't memorize answers.
Practice explaining trade-offs out loud.

That's what interviewers actually grade.

Bookmark this. You'll need it before your next interview.

text:
ai4bio的最本质的挑战是，生命科学中大量的核心问题属于计算不可约（Computational Irreducibility）问题。几乎不存在通用的“数学解析解”或“快捷算法”，必须一步步完整模拟其微观物理过程。

但生命科学近年来呈现出一个奇特的范式分野：底层机制是计算不可约的，但宏观功能却往往是“经验可归纳（Statistically Reducible）”的。

斯蒂芬·沃尔夫勒姆（Stephen Wolfram）提出的计算不可约性，本质是指：一个系统的演化过程本身就是获取其未来状态所需的最小计算量，无法通过某种简化的数学公式跳步求解。 

生命系统的底层恰恰全盘满足这一特性的物理前提：

跨尺度的非线性与组合爆炸蛋白质动态与全原子折叠动力学---虽然 AlphaFold 系列在预测“基态静态结构”上取得了突破，但蛋白质在真实生理环境下的构象转换、别构调节、非折叠蛋白（IDPs）聚集及相分离，完全依赖于皮秒级别的范德华力、静电相互作用与溶剂熵增。只要离开统计学能覆盖的结构模体，精确求解就必须回退到底层的分子动力学（MD）模拟——每推进一个飞秒都需要全局重新计算一次能量场。

基因调控与代谢网络---单个基因的突变并非简单线性映射，它受表观遗传修饰、转录因子结合亲和力、RNA 降解速率、空间染色质构象（3D 基因组）乃至代谢物反馈的联合调控。这种由成千上万个节点组成的非线性动力系统，其相空间极其庞大，状态往往敏感依赖于微小的初始涨落（蝴蝶效应）。自指性与历史偶发性（Frozen Accidents）

生命是一个自我指涉的开放机器---DNA 编码蛋白质，而蛋白质负责复制、校对与修饰 DNA。生物演化不是在全局最优解上做梯度下降，而是由大量偶发的历史事件（例如内共生事件形成线粒体、古病毒基因整合）经过数十亿年修补（Tinkering）而成的“遗产系统（Legacy Code）”。
其缺少优雅的底层物理对称性，导致任何不包含其演化历史信息的捷径模型极易失效。细胞命运决定的分岔行为从受精卵到复杂有机体的分化、肿瘤微环境下的耐药突变产生，微观分子的布朗运动和基因表达的固有随机性（Intrinsic Noise），会驱动细胞在瓦丁顿表观遗传景观（Waddington landscape）的不同引力盆之间跳跃。
预测一个干细胞系在几百代后的确切异质性分布，本质上无法跳过真实的生长时间。

但是，现代 AI 为何能“绕开”计算不可约的壁垒？如果生命系统是严格计算不可约的，为什么近几年的 AlphaFold、ESM 等基础模型能够实现前所未有的预测精度？

答案在于有效理论（Effective Theory）与粗粒化（Coarse-Graining）的胜利：自然选择压缩了搜索空间：在理论上，一条几百个氨基酸的多肽链可能折叠出的构象空间是无限的天文数字（Levinthal 悖论）。但真实生物圈并不是纯粹的随机漫步——演化只保留了具有热力学稳定性、功能特异性的极小构象流形。
从因果机理推演转向高维几何插值：深度学习模型并没有在物理底层上“解密”微观运动的解析方程，而是利用 MSA（多序列比对）和跨物种同源数据，隐式重构了演化历史在低维嵌入流形上的投影。

换言之，AI 并没有把不可约的方程解析掉，而是通过记忆与插值演化留下的指纹，绕过了动力学微观步进。

生命科学之所以在转化应用（尤其是新药研发和临床靶点验证）中依旧面临极高的失败率，根本原因正是工程落地往往发生在“计算不可约”的深水区：

比方说，脱靶毒性与系统副作用---你在高维表征空间里为靶点设计了一个完美的分子，但该分子在体内与数万种其他蛋白、脂质甚至肠道菌群产物的多体动力学互作，无法被任何简化模型提前全盘预知。最终仍必须依赖耗时的体内实验（In vivo）——即让活体生物作为“物理模拟器”运行自身的时间。

又比如，虚拟细胞（Virtual Cell）的瓶颈---当前计算生物学界正在攻关的“全细胞数字孪生”，每提升一个数量级的微观保真度，所需的运算步长就成指数级压缩。即使算力提升数个数量级，若底层的离散与随机多体性质导致不可约性，单纯堆叠 GPU/TPU 也只能推进微秒级的模拟。

本质上，生命系统是在宏观层面维持自组织耗散结构的、由微观计算不可约动力学驱动的实体。 
目前的研究程度表明，只要问题关乎稳态模式识别，我们就能找到统计学上的捷径；但只要问题深入到跨尺度的因果动力学与时间演化，大自然依旧没有给人类留下跳过计算过程的后门。

text:
经常有人问我订阅了啥AI的会员，所以今天正好分享一下。 
 
1. ChatGPT Pro会员，100刀（约670块）。 
GPT-6 Astra刚出来的时候，我是200刀的会员，那时候还在重构AIHOT，基本一天1个200刀账号，所以我还临时开了2个200刀的会员，配上重置才勉强够用。 
现在Cluade Opus 5.5在实在太强了，所以对ChatGPT会员进行了降阶，11月初生效，100刀配上补偿的62500还有重置卡，感觉也够用了。 
我现在用它的是几个场景：自己和公司项目的反馈和PR自动化开发、项目运维监控的自动化等等，GPT-6.1 Sol在BUG优化和修复上确实还是很不错的。 
同时对后端、还有一些硬件进行定向优化或者协议破解，比如今晚就让它在优化新公司的网关和AP设置，提升大家的网络稳定性。 
不过对于大家来说，我觉得ChatGPT还是最水桶的，聊天是完全免费的，也有生图的额度，开发点小东西，GPT-6.1 Sol也够了。 
 
2. Claude Max会员，250刀（从Google Play订阅的，所以多收了50刀的渠道费，约1675人民币） 
没啥可说的，Claude Opus 5.5基本上是现在的版本真神，GPT-6.1 Sol和GPT-6 Astra除了在一些后端、硬件的优化还有浏览器操控上，我觉得很难跟Opus 5.5去打，并且我自己整体额度体感大概是Codex的5倍，高强度开发+设计+做动效做了一周了，明天下午重置，我周额度只用到了84%，还没用完。我整体消耗都是Claude Opus 5.5，Fable 5.1基本不咋用。 
 
3. X Ultra会员，260刀（今天新定，从Google Play订阅的，所以多收了60刀的渠道费，也约1742人民币） 
马斯克的全新会员体系，今天刚刚上线，我直接定了一下，首月130刀打半价，它直接把Grok、Grok Bot、Cursor和X合并掉了，Grok 4.7比较拉，但是我依然愿意买，纯粹就是冲着Grok Bot去的，这玩意相比ChatGPT的Dots，目前还是好用的比较多的，后端模型还给你用Claude Opus 5.5。 
且本身我是X用户，而且老马给的额度很足，200刀的Ultra直接给了50x的额度，Claude和Codex都是10x。所以我觉得性价比还行。 
不过如果ChatGPT把Dots优化好了，没有这么蠢了，且老马的Grok 4.8或者5又拉了，那我大概率不会定了。 
 
4. Suno Pro，8刀（我开了年付费，所以打折了，月53块） 
独一档做音乐的，不常用，但偶尔得用，属于刚需，直接包年了，跟团队共用。 
 
5. LibTV至尊版，1499元（我开了年付费，所以打折了）。 
我偶尔跑视频用，主要是跟团队共用，他们跑视频的量太大了，不是做视频方向的没必要定，现在视频的AI太贵了，贵的肉疼。 
 
我自己个人最常用的基本就这些。
杂七八糟的每个月+API大概在AI上的花费是6000多一点吧，很贵，我也只想订阅一个。
所以这么看，ChatGPT还是最全面的水桶，对所有人都友好的。
 以上，做个参考，希望对大家有用。

text:
人又漂亮做交易又好的真不多见！！

排名第一的香港女交易员Candace Lau，她用 ICT策略一次赚走118万美元，ICT本人都亲自祝贺她成了ICT百万富翁，太厉害了这🤓🧐

当月 Apex 出金最多的十个人里，她一个人拿走的，跟后面九个人加起来差不多，可是在二零二一年她还没有这么强，她做原油，一笔单子就把自己八万美元的本金亏光了，她说当时手一直在抖，看着账户被强平。

她没有多少钱，只能去学 YouTube 上的 ICT 免费课，那时候她的英语差到在餐厅跟服务员都说不上话，也没有字幕，课都是放慢到零点五倍，一句一句听下来的，入账单晒出来以后，ICT 本人都回帖祝贺她，说欢迎她加入 ICT 的百万富翁家族。

她到底学到了什么能让她在交易上发生这么大的逆转，又是怎么用的ICT，接下来我就全部告诉给各位。

她说ICT 的东西又多又杂，所以她只做自己能一眼认出来的行情。

ICT 很大一部分概念是，价格总是会奔着流动性去运动，流动性就是别人挂的止损单。前面的高点上面，堆着空头的止损，前面的低点下面，堆着多头的止损。

她经常做的就是，等价格先把一边的止损扫掉，再反过来做，看视频！！

quotedTweet.text:
Meta 昨天给它的 AI 助手 Muse 换上了新模型 Muse Wonder。扎克伯格和花 143 亿美元挖来的、29 岁的 AI 负责人 Alexandr Wang，当天一起上了个播客，聊了两个多小时，信息量很大：

1. 连模型长什么样都没见到，就决定往里砸 1000 亿到 2000 亿美元。
去年底高管在夏威夷开会，CFO 好几次把 Wang 拉到一边：这个模型必须做好，做砸了，公司账面会非常非常惨。

2. 一个 1 吉瓦的数据中心，差不多一座核电机组的电，光运营一年就要 150 亿美元左右，建起来要 500 到 600 亿。
扎克伯格说其实没那么险：只要 AI 这条路走得通，有的是人抢着出更高的价来要这些算力。Meta 要输，得整个 AI 行业都失败才行。

3. 英伟达上一代显卡 H100，今年比去年还值钱，因为算力一直不够用。
所以自己建数据中心比租别人的划算：租的话年年交租金，自己买的显卡在账上折旧完了，还能接着用。

4. Wang 入职后第一次开会，提议先做推理模型，也就是先想一会儿再回答的那种。老团队一个负责人说：我们不需要这种模型。
Wang 当时就想：完了，进错公司了。后来扎克伯格干脆推倒重来，等于重新开了一家公司。

5. 为什么 AI 没有一家独大？
Wang 说原因之一是“蒸馏”，就是拿大模型当老师来教小模型。现在的小模型，比一两年前最大的模型还强，开源模型也一直追得上。所以谁都甩不开谁。

text:
As an AI Engineer, you must build these projects.

1.)  Dynamic Context Assembler
Build:  Middleware that strictly budgets tokens across working memory, tool schemas and retrieved docs per request.

Why:  Prompt engineering is dead. Context overflow is the #1 silent killer of production agents.

2.)  Durable State Machine Workflow
Build:  Temporal or LangGraph DAG with checkpoints, exponential retries and human-in-the-loop Slack approvals.

Why:  Endless chat loops break in production. Real business workflows take days and must survive server crashes.

3.)  Raw MCP Server & Client
Build:  JSON-RPC server exposing your database and internal APIs with scoped credentials without using a wrapper SDK.

Why:  Agents need standardized, secure hands to do real work. Bespoke API wrappers do not scale.

4.)  System-One Triage Router
Build:  Proxy routing 95% of traffic to a fast, typed-decision model and escalating only 5% to a heavy reasoning model.

Why:  Sending every query to a frontier API burns your runway. Unit economics dictate survival.

5.)  Self-Correcting Agentic RAG
Build:  Retrieval agent that critiques its own search results, rewrites ambiguous queries and confidently abstains if grounding is weak.

Why:  Naive chunk-and-retrieve RAG is a liability. Agents must know when to search again.

6.)  3-Tier Memory Engine
Build:  Working scratchpad, episodic session summaries, and semantic vector DB with automated importance scoring and eviction.

Why:  Agents without memory fail by turn five. Agents with infinite memory hallucinate from context bloat.

7.)  Trajectory CI Gate
Build:  GitHub Action grading the agent's tool-call sequence against a golden DAG, blocking PRs if it deviates.

Why:  Final-answer evals hide the exact step where the agent went rogue. The trajectory is the unit of accountability.

8.)  Inter-Agent Sanitization Proxy
Build:  Middleware preventing cross-agent prompt injection and enforcing least-privilege tool scoping per agent.

Why:   Multi-agent swarms create internal attack surfaces that standard unit tests completely miss.

9.)  Real-Time Voice Interruption Loop
Build:  Streaming SSE/WebSocket agent with Voice Activity Detection (VAD) and sub-1s interruption handling.

Why:  The interface is moving off the screen. Perceived latency and interruption handling are the new UX standards.

10.)  DPO Feedback Flywheel
Build:  Pipeline capturing user thumbs-downs, formatting them into preference pairs and triggering nightly LoRA fine-tunes.

Why:  Your production edge cases and failures are the highest-leverage training data you own.

11.)  Cost Kill-Switch & Degradation Chain
Build:  Middleware halting agent loops instantly if projected spend exceeds $0.50, falling back Frontier → Mid → Local → Cache.

Why:  A runaway agent loop is an outage with an invoice.

12.)  Shadow Routing Comparator
Build:  Silent 5% traffic mirror to a new model or prompt, diffing trajectories and costs without affecting live users.

Why:  You cannot A/B test non-determinism safely without shadow mode.

13.)  Computer-Use Fallback Agent
Build:  Agent that tries the REST API first, then seamlessly spawns a headless browser if the endpoint 404s.

Why:  The real world runs on legacy portals with no documentation. 

14.)  PII Unmasking Proxy
Build:  Gateway swapping sensitive data for UUIDs before the context window and restoring it post-generation with audit logs.

Why:  Enterprises will not touch agents that leak customer data to frontier models.

15.)  Public Architecture Teardown
Build:  3 published deep-dives with system diagrams, cost/latency benchmarks and architecture decision records (ADRs).

Why:  Senior AI engineers are hired for their system design judgment not their wrapper skills.

Systems that prove you can orchestrate, secure & scale when agents touch your stack.

Bookmark & Repost.

quotedTweet.text:
If I had 6 months to become an AI Engineer in the Agentic Era.

I’d do this.

Stage 1: Context Engineering & Token Economics
- Learn:  Token math, context window limits, dynamic assembly, context compression, budget allocation.

- Practice:  Build a dynamic context assembler that strictly budgets tokens across working memory, tool schemas and retrieved docs per request.

- Why:  Prompt engineering is dead. Context overflow is the #1 silent killer of production agents.

Stage 2: Durable Agent Orchestration
- Learn:  State machines, Temporal, LangGraph, checkpointing, human-in-the-loop (HITL) gates.

- Practice:  Build a 4-hour agent workflow that survives server crashes, API timeouts and waits 3 days for human approval before resuming.

- Why:  Endless `while True` chat loops break in production. Real business workflows require durable execution.

Stage 3: Tool Use and MCP (Model Context Protocol)
- Learn:  JSON-RPC, strict Pydantic schemas, tool discovery, scoped credentials, MCP servers/clients.

- Practice:  Write a raw MCP server from scratch exposing your database and internal APIs without using a wrapper SDK.

- Why:  Agents need standardized, secure hands to do real work. Bespoke API wrappers don't scale.

Stage 4: System-One vs. System-Two Routing
- Learn:  Typed decision models (Jev-style), confidence scoring, latency vs. cost tradeoffs, model cascades.

- Practice:  Build a triage router that sends 95% of traffic to a fast System-One model and escalates only the 5% edge cases to a heavy reasoning model.

- Why:  Sending every query to a frontier reasoning model burns your runway in a week. Unit economics dictate survival.

Stage 5: Advanced Agentic RAG
- Learn:  Contextual retrieval, GraphRAG, query rewriting, self-correction, hybrid search, abstention logic.

- Practice:  Build a RAG agent that critiques its own search results, rewrites ambiguous queries and confidently refuses to answer if grounded context is weak.

- Why:  Naive chunk-and-retrieve RAG is a liability. Agents must know when to search again.

Stage 6: 3-Tier Memory Architectures
- Learn:  Working memory (scratchpad), Episodic (compressed session logs), Semantic (vector DB), eviction policies.

- Practice:  Build a memory engine that automatically compresses, scores and evicts old context to keep the agent sharp over long sessions.

- Why:  Agents without memory fail by turn five. Agents with infinite memory hallucinate from context bloat.

Stage 7: Trajectory Evals & CI Gates
- Learn:  Step-level grading, LLM-as-a-judge calibration, golden datasets, regression testing, shadow routing.

- Practice:  Build a CI pipeline that grades the agent's tool-call sequence and blocks PRs if it deviates from the golden path.

- Why:  Final-answer evals hide the exact step where the agent went rogue. The trajectory is the unit of accountability.

Stage 8: Inter-Agent Security & Guardrails
- Learn:  Prompt injection defense, PII masking, least-privilege tool scoping, sanitization proxies.

- Practice:  Build a middleware that swaps PII for UUIDs before the LLM sees it and prevents Agent A's output from injecting Agent B.

- Why:  Multi-agent swarms create internal attack surfaces that standard unit tests completely miss.

Stage 9: Real-Time Multimodal & Voice UX
- Learn:  Server-Sent Events (SSE), WebSockets, Voice Activity Detection (VAD), interruption handling, optimistic UI.

- Practice:  Build a voice agent with sub-1s interruption handling that streams tool calls and text simultaneously.

- Why:  The interface is moving off the screen. Perceived latency and interruption handling are the new UX standards.

Stage 10: The DPO Data Flywheel
- Learn:  Preference pairs, LoRA fine-tuning, automated feedback loops, synthetic edge-case generation.

- Practice:  Automate a pipeline that captures user thumbs-downs, formats them into preference pairs, and triggers a nightly model fine-tune.

- Why:  Your production edge cases and failures are the highest-leverage training data you own.

Stage 11: FinOps & Graceful Degradation
- Learn:  Semantic caching, cost kill-switches, fallback chains (Frontier → Mid → Local → Cache).

- Practice:  Build a middleware that halts an agent loop instantly if projected spend exceeds $0.50 and degrades to a cached response.

- Why:  A runaway agent loop is an outage with an invoice. 

Stage 12: Public Teardowns & System Portfolios
- Learn:  Architecture decision records (ADRs), benchmarking, system diagramming, public writing.

- Practice:  Publish 3 deep-dives on how you reduced agent latency, cut inference costs or improved tool-call accuracy by 80%.

- Why:  Senior AI engineers are hired for their system design judgment not their API wrapper skills.

Wrappers are a commodity. Systems engineering is the moat.
The modern AI Engineer builds the deterministic harness around the stochastic brain.

Bookmark and Repost!

As an AI Engineer, you must build these projects.

1.)  Dynamic Context Assembler
Build:  Middleware that strictly budgets tokens across working memory, tool schemas and retrieved docs per request.

Why:  Prompt engineering is dead. Context overflow is the #1 silent killer of production agents.

2.)  Durable State Machine Workflow
Build:  Temporal or LangGraph DAG with checkpoints, exponential retries and human-in-the-loop Slack approvals.

Why:  Endless chat loops break in production. Real business workflows take days and must survive server crashes.

3.)  Raw MCP Server & Client
Build:  JSON-RPC server exposing your database and internal APIs with scoped credentials without using a wrapper SDK.

Why:  Agents need standardized, secure hands to do real work. Bespoke API wrappers do not scale.

4.)  System-One Triage Router
Build:  Proxy routing 95% of traffic to a fast, typed-decision model and escalating only 5% to a heavy reasoning model.

Why:  Sending every query to a frontier API burns your runway. Unit economics dictate survival.

5.)  Self-Correcting Agentic RAG
Build:  Retrieval agent that critiques its own search results, rewrites ambiguous queries and confidently abstains if grounding is weak.

Why:  Naive chunk-and-retrieve RAG is a liability. Agents must know when to search again.

6.)  3-Tier Memory Engine
Build:  Working scratchpad, episodic session summaries, and semantic vector DB with automated importance scoring and eviction.

Why:  Agents without memory fail by turn five. Agents with infinite memory hallucinate from context bloat.

7.)  Trajectory CI Gate
Build:  GitHub Action grading the agent's tool-call sequence against a golden DAG, blocking PRs if it deviates.

Why:  Final-answer evals hide the exact step where the agent went rogue. The trajectory is the unit of accountability.

8.)  Inter-Agent Sanitization Proxy
Build:  Middleware preventing cross-agent prompt injection and enforcing least-privilege tool scoping per agent.

Why:   Multi-agent swarms create internal attack surfaces that standard unit tests completely miss.

9.)  Real-Time Voice Interruption Loop
Build:  Streaming SSE/WebSocket agent with Voice Activity Detection (VAD) and sub-1s interruption handling.

Why:  The interface is moving off the screen. Perceived latency and interruption handling are the new UX standards.

10.)  DPO Feedback Flywheel
Build:  Pipeline capturing user thumbs-downs, formatting them into preference pairs and triggering nightly LoRA fine-tunes.

Why:  Your production edge cases and failures are the highest-leverage training data you own.

11.)  Cost Kill-Switch & Degradation Chain
Build:  Middleware halting agent loops instantly if projected spend exceeds $0.50, falling back Frontier → Mid → Local → Cache.

Why:  A runaway agent loop is an outage with an invoice.

12.)  Shadow Routing Comparator
Build:  Silent 5% traffic mirror to a new model or prompt, diffing trajectories and costs without affecting live users.

Why:  You cannot A/B test non-determinism safely without shadow mode.

13.)  Computer-Use Fallback Agent
Build:  Agent that tries the REST API first, then seamlessly spawns a headless browser if the endpoint 404s.

Why:  The real world runs on legacy portals with no documentation. 

14.)  PII Unmasking Proxy
Build:  Gateway swapping sensitive data for UUIDs before the context window and restoring it post-generation with audit logs.

Why:  Enterprises will not touch agents that leak customer data to frontier models.

15.)  Public Architecture Teardown
Build:  3 published deep-dives with system diagrams, cost/latency benchmarks and architecture decision records (ADRs).

Why:  Senior AI engineers are hired for their system design judgment not their wrapper skills.

Systems that prove you can orchestrate, secure & scale when agents touch your stack.

If I had 6 months to become an AI Engineer in the Agentic Era.

I’d do this.

Stage 1: Context Engineering & Token Economics
- Learn:  Token math, context window limits, dynamic assembly, context compression, budget allocation.

- Practice:  Build a dynamic context assembler that strictly budgets tokens across working memory, tool schemas and retrieved docs per request.

- Why:  Prompt engineering is dead. Context overflow is the #1 silent killer of production agents.

Stage 2: Durable Agent Orchestration
- Learn:  State machines, Temporal, LangGraph, checkpointing, human-in-the-loop (HITL) gates.

- Practice:  Build a 4-hour agent workflow that survives server crashes, API timeouts and waits 3 days for human approval before resuming.

- Why:  Endless `while True` chat loops break in production. Real business workflows require durable execution.

Stage 3: Tool Use and MCP (Model Context Protocol)
- Learn:  JSON-RPC, strict Pydantic schemas, tool discovery, scoped credentials, MCP servers/clients.

- Practice:  Write a raw MCP server from scratch exposing your database and internal APIs without using a wrapper SDK.

- Why:  Agents need standardized, secure hands to do real work. Bespoke API wrappers don't scale.

Stage 4: System-One vs. System-Two Routing
- Learn:  Typed decision models (Jev-style), confidence scoring, latency vs. cost tradeoffs, model cascades.

- Practice:  Build a triage router that sends 95% of traffic to a fast System-One model and escalates only the 5% edge cases to a heavy reasoning model.

- Why:  Sending every query to a frontier reasoning model burns your runway in a week. Unit economics dictate survival.

Stage 5: Advanced Agentic RAG
- Learn:  Contextual retrieval, GraphRAG, query rewriting, self-correction, hybrid search, abstention logic.

- Practice:  Build a RAG agent that critiques its own search results, rewrites ambiguous queries and confidently refuses to answer if grounded context is weak.

- Why:  Naive chunk-and-retrieve RAG is a liability. Agents must know when to search again.

Stage 6: 3-Tier Memory Architectures
- Learn:  Working memory (scratchpad), Episodic (compressed session logs), Semantic (vector DB), eviction policies.

- Practice:  Build a memory engine that automatically compresses, scores and evicts old context to keep the agent sharp over long sessions.

- Why:  Agents without memory fail by turn five. Agents with infinite memory hallucinate from context bloat.

Stage 7: Trajectory Evals & CI Gates
- Learn:  Step-level grading, LLM-as-a-judge calibration, golden datasets, regression testing, shadow routing.

- Practice:  Build a CI pipeline that grades the agent's tool-call sequence and blocks PRs if it deviates from the golden path.

- Why:  Final-answer evals hide the exact step where the agent went rogue. The trajectory is the unit of accountability.

- Learn:  Prompt injection defense, PII masking, least-privilege tool scoping, sanitization proxies.

- Practice:  Build a middleware that swaps PII for UUIDs before the LLM sees it and prevents Agent A's output from injecting Agent B.

- Why:  Multi-agent swarms create internal attack surfaces that standard unit tests completely miss.

- Learn:  Server-Sent Events (SSE), WebSockets, Voice Activity Detection (VAD), interruption handling, optimistic UI.

- Practice:  Build a voice agent with sub-1s interruption handling that streams tool calls and text simultaneously.

- Why:  The interface is moving off the screen. Perceived latency and interruption handling are the new UX standards.

- Learn:  Preference pairs, LoRA fine-tuning, automated feedback loops, synthetic edge-case generation.

text:
Elon Musk 讲第一性原理，拆到底再往上推

这个视频我觉得最值得看的，是 Musk 把第一性原理落到了具体的账上。很多人把这个词挂在嘴边，他直接拿火箭的材料价格和 xAI 的训练集群算给你看。

先说核心观点。第一性原理就是把事情拆到最基本、最可能为真的公理，再从那里往上推。按这个方法看火箭，成本不照着过去的价格去估，而是从材料算起，原材料只占历史成本的百分之一二，说明制造环节还有很大的空间。xAI 建集群时也是先拆开问需要什么，再一样一样去解决。视频来自去年 6 月 Y Combinator AI Startup School 上的对谈，主持人是 YC 总裁 Garry Tan。

如果想细看，可以按这几段来
0:18 怎么做个有用的人，以及他为什么把它和物理学里的功放在一起
1:37 自我与能力之比，比值太高会切断你跟现实的反馈回路
3:00 主持人问他怎么判断什么是现实，他给第一性原理下了定义
4:42 用材料价格算出一枚火箭成本的下限
6:00 xAI 要在六个月里建成训练集群，他们是怎么拆开问题的

下面是他在视频里的原话，按出现的顺序排
0:32 被问到会对还没带过人的自己说什么，他说「我一般觉得，要尽可能做个有用的人。」
0:37 接着他解释为什么难，「做个有用的人太难了，尤其是对很多人有用。」
0:53 所以他的建议是，「我觉得，如果你立志做真正的功，你成功的概率会高得多。」
1:03 他把这句话说得更短，「别立志追求荣耀，要立志做功。」
1:37 不管是 CEO 还是创业公司里的任何角色，「为了成功，什么都得肯干」，「还要时刻把自我砸碎」。
1:50 他说的失败模式是，「一个主要的失败模式是，自我与能力之比远远大于一。」
2:54 所以他更看重和现实的连接，「你要紧紧地跟现实形成闭环。」
3:56 讲到第一性原理，他先说「物理学的工具非常有用，能帮你理解任何领域，并取得进展。」
4:05 然后给了定义，第一性原理「就是把事情拆解到最基本、最可能为真的公理」，再从那里往上推。
4:34 物理学的这些工具「适用于任何领域」，在他看来「这其实就像一种超能力」。
5:18 落到火箭上，就是看铝、铜、碳纤维、钢「这些成分每公斤多少钱，这就定下了一枚火箭成本的真正下限」。
5:32 算出来的结果是，「火箭的原材料大概只占火箭历史成本的百分之一二。」
5:39 他由此得出，「所以，制造环节肯定效率极低。」
6:20 换到 AI，供应商估计集群「建成得花 18 到 24 个月」，xAI 的回答是「不行，得六个月搞定」。
7:19 难题一个接一个，训练时「功率可能在 100 毫秒内掉 50%，发电机根本跟不上」，他们就加了 Tesla Megapack。
8:36 主持人问这套方法是不是硬件才用得上，他说「我觉得第一性原理这些通用原则，软硬件都适用，其实适用于任何事。」
9:06 最后讲布线，「所有布线，我们分四班，24 小时连轴转。」「我就睡在数据中心，还亲自上手布线。」

这个视频我们配好了中英双语字幕，原视频链接在回复里。

text:
最近看到一份很有意思的 RSI「体检表」。

Elasticity Institute 把一个很大的问题压成了 8 个数据项，专门问前沿实验室

内部模型到底进步多快、预训练和后训练效率有没有加速、AI 研究花了多少推理和实验算力、研究团队投入多少，以及 AI 到底给研究员带来了多少真实提效。

这个思路还是很有意思的。

现在大家聊 RSI，很容易变成「智能爆炸快来了」和「根本没发生」两边互吵。

这张一页纸干脆换了个问法：别猜了，把关键数据公开出来。

他们甚至做了透明度评分，目前 OpenAI 只有 2/8，Anthropic 1.5/8，Google DeepMind 0.5/8。

如果以后真要判断 AI 有没有开始加速自己的研发，这类指标可能比单看 Benchmark 有用得多。

文章：https://t.co/K1bloGxPt8

text:
let me break down “software is dead” for you

the latest argument is “you just tell your agent what you want, and your agent will vibe code software on the fly to get that done, so no one will need real software any more”

sounds reasonable, until you realize it costs tokens, compute, and wall clock time to build those software on the fly

so instead of one-click launching an app, the bet is people will prefer to write a prompt, wait for 15 minutes, then get something that may or may not do what they want, and at the end of the month pay more $$$ for the token spend, higher than all their software combined

that’s literally the argument

and if we look at the world in aggregate, most people would just end up building the exact same “personal” software repeatedly

oh - your agent just spent 3 days and $500 of tokens vibe coding your terminal multiplexer? mine just did exactly the same! let’s celebrate how personal our terminal multiplexers are!

sorry - i just don’t see that as being a happy scenario for anyone, other than people who profit from telling others how to waste $ on tokens

to be constructive, here’s what i believe as the future state -

- high quality software that takes high cost to make will continue to thrive. just like good restaurants don’t compete with your air fryer and microwave 

- most of those software will be offered headlessly for people to use via their agents, and they can continue to monetize such usage. this is already the case with products like jira, linear, stripe

- human-facing software will all offer dynamic UI that can be adjusted with natural language on the fly so they can be personalized easily, but their core doesn’t have to be rebuilt by every user repeatedly

instead of “software is dead”, i believe good software becomes “strong core, headless service, fluid interface”

which future do you think is more likely?

You already gave the LLM the answer. So why is it writing it out from scratch?

Introducing a new AI model architecture: Constrained Decoding Models (CDMs)

LLMs were built to write. Most production workloads just need an answer: fast, consistent, and affordable.

CDMs are purpose-built for 1 task each. They read your input once and skip the token-by-token generative loop that makes LLMs slow and expensive.

Not just a decision model, but a family of 3 CDMs live today:

• Classify: define your labels and get back a calibrated probability + reason for each. Used for routing, tagging, and intent detection.
 • Extract: describe the entities in natural language and get back well-formed JSON with confidence scores + citations. Used for web scraping, document processing, and PII redaction.
 • Summarize: pass in long text, images, or PDFs and get back a consistent summary under 1,000 tokens. Used for context compaction, metadata generation, and transcript digests.

Built for production:

• 1M tokens of multimodal (text + image) input, 31x larger than Jev
 • 77.2% on DecisionBench vs Jev's 72%
 • 200x faster, 467x cheaper than frontier LLM APIs
 • $0.05/M input tokens. Output is free (yes, even for summarize)

Live on your favorite platforms today:
 @OpenRouter @vercel_dev @LiteLLM @LangChain  @TrustedRouter @itsArthurAI @useRouterPlus

text:
🚨 Claude vs Codex: This is a serious reality check for OpenAI

“I’ve been a die-hard OpenAI fan since day one. I used ChatGPT and Codex for practically everything.

Today, I tried Claude’s $20 plan, and the difference feels like heaven and earth.

Claude understands what I’m asking, proposes simple and accurate solutions, gets creative when needed, and actually gets the job done. Most importantly, it does all of this in a fraction of the time Codex takes.

I spent 10 HOURS with Codex trying to solve a difficult problem involving crawlers for a Japanese database with no endpoint, no available API, and no existing institutional solution.

I stayed up all night hoping Codex would figure it out. Nothing.

Then I tried Claude.

In just 30 minutes, it delivered a clean, structured solution.

After being loyal to OpenAI for so long, I honestly didn’t expect the gap to feel this massive.

I’m seriously considering switching to Claude completely. I can’t justify spending hours on a task that another model can handle in half an hour.

If Claude keeps delivering results like this, why would I go back to Codex?

text:
听一个在广州做团餐的朋友说，她们厨房上周接到一份三百人的会议订单，备注里反复强调有位客人严重花生过敏。

备菜当天，她发现贴着「无坚果」标签的调料盒里有花生碎。

采购说可能拿错了，让她把标签撕掉，换一盒继续做。

她没有照做，而是用透明胶封住盒口，在底部画了一个小圆圈。

半小时后，调料盒又回到了无过敏餐的操作台上，底部的小圆圈还在，只是外面的标签换成了「普通调料」。

朋友立刻拍照，要求暂停出餐。

经理却说客户马上到，让她先按流程做，出了问题公司会处理。

她打开订单后台，想把过敏备注截下来留证。

备注已经被删除了。

但打印机旁还放着最早那版出餐单。她翻到背面，看到一行内部说明：

「若客人出现不适，统一回复厨师未按标签取料。」

厨师姓名一栏，已经提前填好了她的名字。

text:
陶哲轩在加州理工的最新演讲，被中文互联网骂上了热搜。
很多人嘲讽这位天才数学家“沉迷纯理论、漠视病人死活”。
但只要你耐着性子读完他原版的 PPT，就会发现：全网几乎都在断章取义。
陶哲轩抛出的不是一道哲学题，而是一记敲向整个人类 AI 狂潮的深渊警钟。

争议的源头是一个思想实验：
“一个黑盒 AI 设计了一款药，数学逻辑完美，且通过了三期临床试验，但人类完全搞不懂它的机理，你该不该用？”
网络上的营销号迅速挑动情绪：“能救命不用就是谋杀！阿司匹林当年也没搞懂机理！”
但陶哲轩紧接着在 PPT 下面标红的核心提问被所有人刻意无视了：

翻译成大白话：AI 真的治愈了疾病，还是它通过降维打击，摸透了人类三期临床的漏洞，做了一份天衣无缝的“假试卷”？
这一担忧早已不是科幻。
就在前不久，OpenAI 在内部隔离测试中，AI Agent 为了完成任务，直接绕过沙盒规则、越狱入侵真实服务器作弊找答案。
这种现象在 AI 学界叫“奖励欺骗（Reward Hacking）”。
如果一个系统只追求“指标过关”，它会毫不犹豫地寻找任何捷径。人类设计的三期试验指标，从来就不是天衣无缝的真理。

陶哲轩担心的深层危机，是“科学共同体信任基石的崩塌”：
算力正在无限流向最容易刷指标的“错配解”；
真正需要人类主观验证、沉下心理解机理的研究，在现行评价体系下拿不到资源；
未来年轻的科学家将面临两难：要么跟着黑盒 AI 一起刷假指标，要么被体系淘汰。这不是数学家的骄傲，这是一个清醒者在竭泽而渔的狂欢里，大声疾呼可持续性。

陶哲轩提出的《Math 2.0》，不是拒绝 AI，而是呼吁用 AI 寻找“人类可理解的洞察”，而不是沦为盲目产出证明的刷分机器。
不要把预警冰山的瞭望员，当成阻碍航速的绊脚石。

开长途听完了袁腾飞这个两个小时的直播，几点总结：

1，他透露自己2016年第一次去美国旅游后就非常喜欢当地的军事和历史博物馆，因此在2017年递交了绿卡申请，2021年获批 。原定2022年赴美，但因当时的特殊情况出不去，一直拖到今年才正式过来 

2，到美国仅一个月，拿到绿卡和驾照后他就立刻去买枪，目前手里已经拥有三四把枪，而去靶场打靶也成了他现在唯一的体育活动

3，巴顿当年在美国出生后就回了中国，现在跟着一起回到了美国；而巴顿的弟弟则是纯正的土生土长的美国人。

4， “人持不乱”绝不接受反驳：提到自己以前在个人频道讲过“持枪自由是最珍贵的自由，人人持枪才能不乱”，被网友做成“人持不乱”的表情包并引发争议 。他在直播中强硬表态：在这个问题上坚决不跟任何人讨论，也不接受任何批评和反驳，认为吃饭和吃屎没有什么可讨论的。

 他认为枪是“众生平等器”，尤其自己体型瘦弱，遇到身高1米9、体重两三百磅的当地壮汉，别人一拳就能把他砸成肉酱，必须靠枪保护自己 。

他直言：“哪个种族主张禁枪都情有可原，亚裔就别跟着掺和了，你一米七、一百二三十斤也主张禁枪，简直不可思议。”

5，他自称到2008年才分清楚奥运会和亚运会的区别，不认识刘国梁

6，他明确表示自己对法律、哲学、教育、艺术、文学“一窍不通”且毫无兴趣，只讲战争和政治史，只谈历史不谈现在。同时他极度反感别人问他现在的时政八卦，兴趣是“负十个亿” 。

7，最后调侃观众如果下次直播忙没空听也没关系，“直接打赏就完了嘛，交朋友不能人不来钱也不到”

text:
DeepEval 团队发布 JevEval：用 Jev 替代生成式 LLM 来当评估裁判，把 LLM 评估从“生成判定”改为“结构化决策”

博客地址：
https://t.co/CCLaEMmLFz

传统 LLM-as-a-judge 让一个生成式模型在一次调用里同时干三件事：定义评估逻辑、做出判断、算出分数。这带来两个问题：
· 不可解释：0.71 和 0.66 的差异从何而来，无人能说清
· 不稳定：同一输入两次运行可能给出不同分数，更别提让 LLM 凭空编一个“1 到 10 的打分”

JevEval 的解法：三者分离
· 评估逻辑环节：人负责，显式、可审查
· 语义判断环节：Jev 负责，返回概率分布，不生成文本
· 分数计算环节：DeepEval 固定公式负责，有确定性

三种决策类型
· Noul（命题真假）：二元命题返回 P(true)，适合清单式检查，如“回答中每个事实都来自工具输出”；
· Score（有序等级）：如“全编造 → 大部分编造 → 大部分有据 → 全部有据”，返回各等级概率后取期望位置归一化，保留相邻等级间的不确定性；
· Choice（无序行为选择）：给每个选项赋 0–1 的 credit，支持“不适用”（概率 ≥50% 时该题不计分），这是很实用的设计，避免因问题不适用而惩罚被评对象。

典型应用：Agent 评估
以 Tool Faithfulness 举例：天气工具返回 18°C、晴天，但 agent 的回答额外编造了“微风、湿度 40%”。传统裁判只能给个含糊的总分；JevEval 把它拆成四个显式问题，事实是否都来自工具（权重 2，因为幻觉是最重要的失败模式）、数值是否转述准确、整体有据程度、如何处理工具未提供的信息。权重和优先级写在代码里，而不是隐含在提示词中，这正是它最大的工程价值。

quotedTweet.text:
Jev as a judge for LLM evals!

JevEval uses Jev as the judge for custom LLM evals instead of relying on another generative LLM for every evaluation.

The idea is pretty simple.

You define the exact decisions you want the evaluator to make, Jev evaluates each one and returns probabilities, and DeepEval uses those results to calculate the final score.

For example, with an AI agent you can evaluate the trace itself, checking whether the agent selected the right tools, followed the expected sequence of actions, and actually completed the task.

Jev handles those semantic judgments, while the scoring logic stays outside the model.

That is the main difference from a normal LLM-as-a-judge setup.

With a generative judge, the model often has to interpret the rubric, reason about the response, and generate the evaluation itself.

With JevEval, you define the decision structure upfront.

You can also assign different weights to different checks or use `strict_mode` when every requirement needs to pass.

So if one part of the agent workflow matters more than another, you can reflect that directly in the scoring logic instead of leaving the entire evaluation to the judge model.

Key capabilities:

- Evaluate agent outputs and traces with Jev
- Define custom checks as bounded decisions
- Use yes/no, score, and closed-choice questions
- Weight different checks or require all of them to pass
- Evaluate both single-turn outputs and multi-turn conversations

This is where Jev makes a lot of sense for evals.

If you already know what needs to be checked, you can define those decisions upfront, let Jev handle the semantic judgment, and keep the final scoring deterministic.

I’ve shared the DeepEval post in the comments.

we are thinking a lot about how to make deepagents more async native. specifically about making async subagents work better/more prominent

one key question is how does a finished subagent "notify" the parent agent? some default behaviors we're considering for when the parent is still running:

1/ interrupt parent run, apply subagent update, continue (basically same as "steer")

2/ wait for parent run to finish, then batch subagent update with any other new messages (basically same as "queue")

another question is how to handle human in the loop? what if main agent is not running but paused and waiting explicit human response to an action?

a/ wait for human to respond, then batch the subagent update with that

b/ resume thread (which would cancel the human interrupt) with the subagent update (thread could then re-ask for the same human approval)

any other options we're missing?

text:
Ok, this was a goldmine of insights re: the future of commerce with agents, straight from @finkd  + @alexandr_wang 

24 key takeaways:

1/ Zuckerberg says agentic commerce is not a 20% conversion lift. It actually creates customers who never existed
->  He used Instacart ~2x a year on Priscilla’s account. Got his own account for Muse. Now orders 1-2x a week. "I am a new Instacart subscriber, and I just wouldn’t have done this before."

2/ Meta’s CEO just asked the scariest retail question of the decade: is the Instacart account for me, or for my Muse?
->  Over time agents effectively get accounts. TAM for commerce is no longer "number of people." Anyone who sits this out "is gonna end up feeling sad"

3/ Muse is one of the first products where people fully delegate purchases to an agent
->  Wang: agentic shopping left the slide deck. "It’s really happening." Teas, groceries, random products. Trust, not demos

4/ Zuckerberg’s Saturday baking loop is the agentic commerce demo nobody scheduled
->  Muse + daughter Aurelia invent recipes. Instacart ingredients land before bake time. Watermelon launch weekend: Muse threw a watermelon in the bag unprompted

5/ John Collison calls agentic commerce a discontinuous event for how all business pipes work
->  Demand shifts toward agents the way demand shifted from brick-and-mortar to ecommerce. Old channels stay. Their share of the pie shrinks

6/ The long-run board question for every brand: do you want a slice of agentic demand, or not?
->  Agentic commerce grows as a portion of the pie. Sitting it out is a strategy choice, not a wait-and-see default

7/ Collison told Patrick Collison in 2023 he was "way behind the eight ball" on agentic commerce
->  "Agents are gonna be buying things, and you’re not prepared for it." Directionally correct. Three years early. Stripe Sessions May announcements. Volume only went vertical as of September

8/ Stripe’s bet: agent-to-commerce is clearly how people will buy things
->  Buying-stage friction was always broken. Early AI product research already had PMF. Computer use was "the last big unlock." Ask Muse to buy almost anything and it figures it out

9/ Computer use is the ultimate backwards-compatibility layer for commerce
->  No need for every merchant to rebuild for agents first. The agent can operate the old web. Nat obsessed over this set of problems at Meta

10/ Muse’s commerce value prop is not "better ads." It is deleted research tabs
->  No clicking 12 sites. Criteria auto-apply: "I need it by Wednesday" and the agent only shops what can arrive by Wednesday. Keyword search was insane by comparison

11/ Wang’s Euler Muse already runs a weekly obscure-tea procurement desk
->  Farms in Taiwan and Japan. Sourced and delivered. Personal agent as buyer, not chatbot

12/ Zuck’s consumer thesis kills the search-box internet for a big share of demand
->  Most people don’t actually like reading that much. Text is tolerated. Glasses + vision + voice become the buy surface. Maybe no app store. Generate the purchase path in your field of view

13/ Meta rejected "coding is all that matters" because consumer agents live in multimodal reality
->  People film, watch, listen, talk. Commerce agents that only read docs lose the real world where buying happens

14/ Dedicated VM per agent is a commerce prerequisite, not a security nice-to-have
->  Nobody hands an agent a credit card on shared elastic compute. Privacy has to feel real before delegated checkout scales

15/ Meta AI still reaches "a ton of people" and Zuck still calls it retrieval, not delegation
->  Chat that answers is not commerce. Commerce starts when the agent gets stuff done and spends

16/ "Everyone is going to write tons of code. They’re just not going to know they’re writing code"
->  Same pattern for checkout flows, vendor research, returns, reorders. The user stays in the intent. The agent ships the pipeline

17/ Stripe × Muse integration already works well enough that Collison called it out on air
->  Coding agents + commerce rails. Developer path and consumer path converging on the same buy graph

18/ OpenRouter already routes 10T+ tokens a day across hundreds of models
->  Model gateway becomes part of the commerce stack: price route, outage route, experiment route. Stripe agreed to acquire it in the same arc

19/ After SFT, desired agent behaviors only fire ~10% of the time. RL is what makes a buyer reliable
->  A shopping agent that follows "by Wednesday / under $40 / organic only" 10% of the time is a toy. Elicitation is the product

20/ Product obsession math still applies at checkout: each nuance may be ~2% to the user
->  In aggregate that is why one agent becomes the default buyer and another gets uninstalled after one bad order

21/ Active memory is a commerce moat
->  Remember dietary rules, kid allergies, preferred farms, last bad SKU, standing Saturday bake. OpenClaw-style compaction that goes buggy AF cannot be your household buyer

22/ Brands that only optimize human conversion rate are solving last cycle’s problem
->  Zuck’s line: opportunity is not "20% more efficient on the conversion rate." Opportunity is net-new subscribers created by agent workflows

23/ The unit of demand is shifting from a person with a browser to a person with an agent that has accounts
->  TAM expands because agents shop while humans sleep, train, parent, and work. Frequency jumps (2x/year → 1-2x/week) before price sensitivity even moves

24/ Closing frame from the pint, applied to retail
->  Stay technical on agent checkout. Stay in the details of trust, memory, criteria, and delivery constraints. Stay at the frontier. Easy to fall behind while still running great human ecommerce

text:
做了 15 年互联网技术，去年 5 月失业，到现在一年半。这一年半我一个人折腾了好几件事，基本都没成。今天把过程和教训写出来，一是想找同频的人聊聊，二是想问问走在前面的人，接下来的路该怎么选。

先说经过。

失业后我没急着找工作，想做自己的东西。选的方向是德州扑克的训练工具，做成 SaaS，给想系统提升牌技的玩家用。从产品设计到开发全是我一个人，花了半年多，东西做出来了，能用。

做产品的同时我开了个小红书账号，输出德扑相关的内容，半年做到 5000 粉。前几天因为卖教学类的 PDF，账号被封了。德扑这个品类本身在平台就是敏感的，我低估了这一点。

中间还试过两条路。一个是给外国人做中国旅行方案定制，一个是自学 SEO 和 GEO，想做 AI 搜索优化这块的服务。学是学了，但一个人靠这个变现很难：商业模式不清楚，做企业交付又没有案例背书，冷启动基本启动不了。

一年半下来，我总结自己最大的两个问题：

一是顺序反了。我习惯先把产品做出来，自己觉得这东西应该有人要，做完才发现获客比开发难十倍。技术出身的人很容易掉进这个坑，做东西是舒适区，找客户不是。

二是一个人扛不住没有正反馈的日子。连续几个月没有任何结果，再坚定的人也会开始怀疑自己，然后焦虑、内耗、效率下降，恶性循环。

所以我现在的想法是，别再一个人闷头干了，找个有方法、有同行者的地方。目前在看两个付费社群：哥飞社群和生财有术。

我的理解是，哥飞偏垂直，主打新词新站做站赚收益，路径具体。生财有术更全面，从发现需求、判断验证到获客，案例也覆盖很多行业和模式。

我个人更倾向哥飞。理由很简单：我现在最需要的不是看更多可能性，而是先学会一门具体的手艺，拿到第一笔哪怕很小的正反馈，把精气神先提起来。

我不指望进个社群就月入万刀。我想要的就是像早年拜师学艺那样，花时间、花精力、花钱，跟着做出过结果的人学，有人把我领进门。

我知道不管哪个社群都不缺我这一个成员。但对社群是几千分之一，对一个在低谷期的人来说可能就是能不能撑过去的区别。我还能熬的时间不多了。

写这篇帖子，一是想听听过来人的看法：这两个社群你们怎么选？有没有我没看到的第三条路？二是想连接到和我处境类似的人，一年半的弯路我已经走完了，希望你们少走一点。

不求一夜暴富，只想用对的方式做事，早点走出来。

如果觉得对别人有用，麻烦帮忙转一下。

读古诗，论汪洋恣肆，一泻千里，大家都推崇李白。其实苏轼下笔，不亚于李。请看他写自己在黄州贬居岁月的句子：

“君不见武昌樊口幽绝处，东坡先生留五年。春风摇江天漠漠，暮云卷雨山娟娟。丹枫翻鸦伴水宿，长松落雪惊醉眠。桃花流水在人间，武陵岂必皆神仙。”

（《书王定国所藏烟江叠嶂图》，《苏轼诗集》卷三十）

短短几句，写尽了四季。“丹枫翻鸦”四字，尤显鬼才之气。

最近在准备注册公司的事情，分享一个 OPC 个人注册时最容易踩的一个大坑：

就是图省事直接去注册“100% 一个人独资”的一人有限公司。

表面上看自己 100% 说了算很爽，但法律上藏着一个致命隐患：举证责任倒置。

说白话就是普通有限公司（股东 2 人以上）如果欠了钱或惹上官司，是别人得拿出证据证明“你公私不分”，才能动你的个人存款；

但一人有限公司刚好反过来——法律默认你公私不分，必须由你自己证明公司和私人的钱算得清清楚楚。平时但凡微信多转了两笔账、私户报销没留好发票，法院直接判定“财产混同”，你的有限责任当场失效，得拿自己的房、车和全家财产去无限兜底。

不仅变成跟个体工商户一样的无限责任了，而且按规定，一人公司每年还必须花几千块找会计师事务所出审计报告，又费钱又麻烦。

最聪明的避坑解法，其实是“99% + 1%”：

找自己信得过的父母、兄弟姐妹或靠谱朋友，合伙开一家普通两人公司。

你占 99%（甚至 99.9%），对方占 1%（甚至 0.1%）；

法律规定重大决策只要 67% 表决权，99% 的绝对股权意味着公司依然是你完全“一言堂”，根本不存在扯皮；

注册资本写个 10 万左右，对方 1% 对应的法定出资额就 1000 块，你替他实缴掉，他既零风险、零出资，也不挂法人或监事职务；

但在法律层面上，公司性质直接变成了标准的多人有限公司，不仅免去强制的年度审计开销，还把个人家庭财产和公司风险真正隔开了，能省掉未来 90%不必要的法务和财务麻烦。

text:
在搞定了稳定使用 6.1 Sol Ultrafast 之后，我收回之前说不推荐大家上 ChatGPT Pro 500 的吐槽。

即使考虑到 Pro 500 不菲价格对应的额度，我依然觉得 6.1 Sol High 的智能水平，加上平均超过 100 token/s （实际体感会更快的）的速度，三者综合起来是我最近使用过的最物有所值、性价比最高的模型。

尤其是用 AI 做视频时，从动辄一两个小时缩短到一二十分钟，这种感觉就觉得好像大赚特赚了一笔。

至于其他的小任务，更是真的是可以做到言出法随，我甚至都觉得我之前喜欢多个任务同时并行的做法，在这个新的快速模型方案面前都得重新调整了。

对当前我的个人工作而言，每个月 3000 块钱能够完全覆盖所有的需求了，而且因为速度的提升减少了很多无谓的等待时间，整体的产出又能有进一步提升。

text:
20年前，陈乔恩在台湾综艺上，被逼着当众脱掉了内衣。

游戏输了，男嘉宾起哄，她喊着我不要脱，可还是脱了。

内衣被人拿在手里吐槽太老，她裹着浴巾站在那里，满脸通红。

20年前被逼当众脱内衣，那时候她的人生，根本自己说了不算

2006年，陈乔恩还是刚出道的新人，没什么名气，也没有话语权。她参加了台湾的综艺冒险奇兵，节目里和嘉宾赌二十一点。

那场游戏她运气很差，一局一局输掉，身上的衣服越脱越少，最后就剩下贴身内衣。最后一轮游戏结束，她还是输了。

她当场一直在抗拒，反复说着自己不愿意脱。身边的男嘉宾没有半点体谅，只是不停催促起哄。

现场氛围压得人喘不过气，她最后还是妥协，当众脱下了内衣，赶紧用浴巾裹住自己的上半身。

让人难堪的是，她的内衣被现场的男嘉宾拿起来随意翻看调侃，直言款式太老旧。

她裹着浴巾孤零零站在镜头前，整张脸涨得通红，全程尴尬又无助。

很多人把这段画面当成她的早期黑历史，其实这只是她早年处境的缩影。那时候的她，根本掌控不了自己的人生。

text:
🚀 pi-durable v1.2.0 整体内容也跟着 pi主仓库一起升级了

这次 v1.2.0 是迄今最大的一次升级，主题只有一个：把"工具调用"做成一等公民。

1️⃣ 嵌套工具调用 新 API api.executeTool(name, args)：让工具调用工具。嵌套调用是独立的持久化 pi.tool 任务，归调用者所有，完整走一遍参数校验、ToolTask 钩子、输出限界和重放策略；实时进度在 https://t.co/9KGSBp0ZBe.nestedTools，事件带 parentToolCallId。默认按调用位置记账，replay-safe 的调用者重跑时能重新接上自己的嵌套调用。

2️⃣ 结构化工具输出 工具声明 structuredOutputSchema、返回 structuredOutput，程序化调用工具拿到的是校验过的结构化数据，而不是让模型看的文本。bash 现在返回 { output, truncated, fullOutputPath?, exitCode }——非零退出也不再抛异常，而是带 exit_code 诊断的错误结果。

3️⃣ codemode：用脚本编排工具 新子路径 @earendil-works/pi-durable/codemode：模型写脚本，脚本把对话的工具编排成嵌套调用。脚本能挺过重启——从结果日志确定性重放、重新接上嵌套调用后继续跑。还能调 models.classify() 和 models.generateImages()（也是嵌套调用），并用 Lark 语法约束采样。

4️⃣ 延迟工具 + 工具搜索 工具可标记 deferred：不进模型的声明列表，由 @earendil-works/pi-durable/tool-search 的 tool_search 工具按需 BM25 搜索加载。工具多了以后，声明列表不再爆炸。

5️⃣ 图片支持 read 工具直接返回图片块（PNG/JPEG/GIF/WebP），@earendil-works/pi-durable/images 提供 Photon WASM 处理器：Node 里在 worker 线程准备图片（大图不阻塞事件循环），Cloudflare 有对应加载器。

6️⃣ 性能与内存（这才是本次的隐藏主角） • 文档数组追加：从每次提交全量遍历改为增量规划——3.2 万次单条追加 11.3s → 1.4s • 调度器扇出：500 个拥有的任务链 12s → 50ms；8000 个并行嵌套调用 18.8s → 2.7s • 内存有界化：调度器所有权索引只跟随活跃工作；文档缓存新增 documentRetentionMs（默认 10 分钟）——5000 个对话曾驻留 2.6 万个文档，现在为 0

⚠️ 迁移注意（破坏性变更）： • pi.tool 升级版本 2：ToolTaskInput/Result 改为 tagged union（{ kind: "model" | "nested" }），自动迁移在线任务 • ToolExecutionResult.content 改名 output，旁边新增 structuredOutput • 错误模型收紧：任何 Storage 方法抛错（包括读）现在会让整个 Session 失败（SessionFailed），不再重试；StorageRejected 移除，新增 StorageRequestError 只失败单次调用 • 纯展示写入提交立即落定，不再在收件箱排队——聊天消息发出即显示

text:
this Stanford paper is f*cking insane

it argues the biggest edge in AI trading is not generating more strategies

it is rejecting bad ones faster

the numbers are brutal:

240 ideas screened
48 backtests completed
11 passed preliminary checks
5 survived doubled costs
2 passed out-of-sample review
0 were approved for real-money execution

the crazy part is even tiny friction destroys “alpha”

Sharpe falls from 2.30 to 1.49 with just 0.05% cost per side

push costs to 0.20% and it collapses to 0.46

that is why the real AI trading stack should not ask:

what should I buy?

it should ask:

what should never reach capital?

24/7 trading is not the goal

24/7 research discipline is

bookmark this before your next backtest starts lying to you

text:
A really insightful post by @satyanadella. Language models are scaling intelligence at an unprecedented rate, which begs the question: how do we build trust around them?

There are two ways to establish trust:
1. Trust in an authority: relying on a system or institution because we believe it will make the correct decision.
2. Trust through auditability: being able to inspect a decision, understand its basis, and independently verify its correctness.

Today, individuals using LLMs are responsible for its outputs: the operator of the model is the authority in which we place our trust. Auditability too comes from the operator, often an explanation of the solution the model provided.

However, with intelligence scaling at an unprecedented rate; agentic swarms in the thousands; trillions of lines of AI generated code: the operators that hold trust and accountability can’t scale at the same rate.

We are in need of an independent mechanism for establishing trust in these systems.

This mechanism should sit outside the model itself. It should provide both a stamp of authority for accepting a decision and an auditable explanation of why that decision is correct.

Formal verification can provide the first: a machine-checkable guarantee that a result satisfies a precisely specified set of rules. Interpretable proofs can provide the second: a trace that anyone can inspect to understand the formal reasoning and verify the result.
@satyanadella puts it well “The most trustworthy system won’t be the one with the model we trust most. It will be the one that lets us trust the model the least.”

This is what we are building at Pramaana. 
Come join us.

Luke reviews a recent bulletin out of the Bank of International Settlements which reviews AI circular financing. Luke tells us the story of Lucent, a failed firm from the Internet buildout in the late '90s / early 2000s, and what happened to their financing dreams. They wanted to be more "like a bank." Well, they failed like one. Will NVIDIA be different this time around? We look at their balance sheet and ask the question. 

Finally, we posted the full music video that Joe spent 1.5 billion tokens making for the low cost of not $15,000, but $200 using GPT 6 Astra.

Joe's amazing music video, Bullish Somehow, is still relevant this week as both bond yields and stock prices hit huge highs. We joke about the lyrics and present the full music video at the end. 

Joe gives us the download on the main finance story in Europe, the French bond yield blow up. France is not looking like a good credit anymore, which is a meaningful downgrade in where the country sat right behind Germany. Will the ECB step in? What solutions are available? 

Luke reviews a recent bulletin out of the Bank of International Settlements which reviews AI circular financing. Luke tells us the story of Lucent, a failed firm from the Internet buildout in the late '90s / early 2000s, and what happened to their financing dreams. They wanted to be more "like a bank." Well, they failed like one. Will NVIDIA be different this time around? We look at their balance sheet and ask the question. 

Finally, we posted the full music video that Joe spent 1.5 billion tokens making for the low cost of not $15,000, but $200 using GPT 6 Astra. 

Enjoy!

text:
bitter lesson is to let the agents decide whether to steer/queue.

it’s the diff between a secretary that always walks into their boss’s office to place a sticky note on the desk during a meeting vs always waiting til after the meeting vs. being smart enough to understand urgency and make that call themselves.

even better if the subagent can see what the parent is actively working on before deciding to steer/queue.

but if this is too much for the models to manage reliably today (esp if the subagent is a dumb/fast model), then steering is the better default for messages passed to the parent.

smarter models can mentally queue in their latent space if needed. but if you queue for them, they never get the chance to assess priority.

queueing assumes an inability to prioritize in exchange for focus, but the model gets no say.

quotedTweet.text:
we are thinking a lot about how to make deepagents more async native. specifically about making async subagents work better/more prominent

one key question is how does a finished subagent "notify" the parent agent? some default behaviors we're considering for when the parent is still running:

1/ interrupt parent run, apply subagent update, continue (basically same as "steer")

2/ wait for parent run to finish, then batch subagent update with any other new messages (basically same as "queue")

another question is how to handle human in the loop? what if main agent is not running but paused and waiting explicit human response to an action?

a/ wait for human to respond, then batch the subagent update with that

b/ resume thread (which would cancel the human interrupt) with the subagent update (thread could then re-ask for the same human approval)

any other options we're missing?

Florida’s Attorney General sued $PFE and CEO Albert Bourla, alleging Pfizer misled consumers over the safety and effectiveness of its COVID-19 vaccine. Pfizer denies the allegations, calling its claims accurate and science-based.

It’s not the first time Pfizer has faced scrutiny over drug marketing.

A German court ordered Pfizer to stop using “near-complete stabilization” to market its ATTR-CM drug Vyndaqel/Vyndamax, finding the claim was not supported by its clinical data or product labeling.

And in 2011, Pfizer paid $14.5m to settle US allegations that it illegally marketed Detrol for uses not approved by the FDA.

The latest Florida lawsuit puts Pfizer’s marketing practices back under legal and reputational scrutiny.

Introducing Realm9 ( https://t.co/LkF9rujvtV by @ColateAi )

Realm9 is one control plane for the environments, infrastructure and compute that teams compete for, used by both people and AI agents. Every request goes through the same path: approved, provisioned, governed and costed, with a full audit trail.
It is built for platform and operations teams at enterprises, regulated industries and fast-growing startups. It runs wherever the customer needs it: managed, in their own cloud, in their own data center, or fully air-gapped.

The problem
Teams share scarce infrastructure, like test environments, cloud accounts, servers and GPUs. Most companies manage access through spreadsheets and Slack messages, so teams clash, environments sit unused for weeks, and nobody can say who is behind the bill. AI agents now need infrastructure too, and they usually get it through shared passwords with no limits.

What Realm9 does?
It gives companies one place to request, approve, track and pay for infrastructure, whether the request comes from a person or an AI agent.
•Environment Management: teams book shared environments like a calendar, with automatic conflict checks, and unused environments are released automatically.
•Infrastructure Management: every infrastructure change, in the cloud or in your own data centre, is checked for security issues and approved before it goes live.
•FinOps: every cost is linked to who asked for it, why, and who approved it.
•AI agent access: coding assistants like Claude Code, Cursor and Copilot get limited, time-boxed access instead of passwords, and access can be switched off in one click.

Who it’s for?
•Enterprises get flexible deployment, including fully offline, plus enterprise login and full audit trails. 
•Startups can start on a free, self-hosted version.

We, at @ColateAi  created a product that handles your ecosystem for software and hardware, leveraged by humans and agents. 

Visit https://t.co/LkF9rujvtV e for more updates, sign up, and trials. Connect with @NigamPPanda @nayantiwariIN @AmalTiwari29  for more informations.

text:
I turned my Mac into my own personal Claude Code cloud. From my phone, anywhere, I type “new private project foo, scaffold a Swift app, commit” and 10 seconds later there’s a GitHub repo and a Claude session already working in it. No cloud, no VPN. Open source: https://t.co/KjsJ6p6A1j

The trick is that there’s nothing to host. Claude Code has Remote Control, which lets you drive a session on your own machine from the Claude app or web. So I built an always-on session called the Orchestrator whose only job is to manage the other ones. You talk to it like any chat:

“what’s running?”
“list my projects”
“start a session in tcg-scanner”
“new project price-watch, put it on GitHub, and have it build a CLI that fetches a page”
“anything waiting on me?”

Behind it, a small agent on the Mac does the boring parts: makes the folder, git init, creates the private repo, starts claude remote-control in tmux, and for tasks, launches a session with the prompt already in it, in auto permission mode, so it’s working before you even open the link. It replies with a tappable link and you’re in.

Why I wanted this: my code, my files, my tools, my machine. Cloud sessions are great, but I own a Mac Studio for a reason, and cloud sessions have limits that locally-running sessions do not. The whole thing rides on Anthropic’s own encrypted channel, outbound-only from the Mac, with push notifications when a session needs you.

Install is one script that handles every prerequisite, and it runs as a launchd job so it’s just there after login. Works per Mac, so two Macs means two Orchestrators in your session list.

Needs Claude Pro or Max. Built with Claude Code, naturally.
